ranking.note: Raised to P1: release binaries silently lose BTI/PAC/CET hardening markers, a security defect in shipped artifacts, on par with #35765's release-integrity failure
Moved up: it restores deterministic release builds that are currently broken on the 32.x branch, the most time-bound item in the P2 group
Placed ahead of #25573 because its card states it supplies the CI infrastructure that static-linux builds need
Raised to P2 and moved up for consistency with #36589: both are 32.x release-branch backports needed for the 32.2 point release
Raised to P2: it is the compiler-baseline step the C++23 RFC (#36033, P2) depends on, so it cannot sit below it
Raised to P2 and moved up: adds supported-platform (Windows) build/run support for multiprocess and is a stated prerequisite for #28722
Moved up: it fixes an actual build failure of the code-signing environment, which is release tooling rather than hygiene
Slightly lower than its score position: target restructuring with no breakage fixed ranks below actual depends/release build failures
Kept P3: Boost remains a depends package via MultiIndex, so no dependency is actually dropped from the build
Moved up: fixes a concrete platform test failure and adds per-PR CI enforcement for a recurring failure mode
Moved up: fixes a real Guix configure failure, which outranks warning-flag and convenience work in this category
Moved up: removes a privileged-container requirement from CI, a recurring infrastructure burden
Moved up: release-process monitoring that prevents a signing certificate from blocking an unplanned release
Moved down: speculative CI automation with no demonstrated failure it would have caught
Moved down: binary size saving is real but smaller in consequence than CI and platform fixes above it
Moved down: packaging convenience with no breakage behind it ranks below CI reliability and platform work
Moved down: narrow path-quoting coverage on one CI job
Raised to P3 to match #36844: same IWYU enforcement series, and it is the downstream half of that chain

inconsistencies: #36589 and #36727 are both 32.x release-branch backport sets for the same point release; review #36589 first since it restores builds that are currently broken, then #36727.
Chain: #36042 (GCC 13 minimum) is the concrete step that the C++23 RFC #36033 assumes; review #36042 first, as #36033 is explicitly WIP/RFC and depends on the baseline decision.
Chain: #36082 (Guix builds in CI) is cited as the infrastructure needed to introduce static Linux builds in #25573; reviewing #36082 first de-risks #25573.
Chain: #36844 unblocks #36808 (both IWYU enforcement); #36844 must be reviewed first, and they were originally split across P3/P4 despite being the same work.

Chain among the warning-flag PRs by one author: #36743 is the base for #36781, and #35911 builds on #36087, #36819 includes #36501. These touch overlapping broad swaths of files and are best reviewed as a batch in dependency order rather than individually.

#35068 (depends CMake package discovery) and #35765 (depends local source archives) both fix correctness of the depends system; #35765 is the more severe (silent wrong source tree) and should be reviewed first, but #35068 directly affects native_libmultiprocess builds relevant to #32387.
Multiprocess cluster: #32387 (Windows IPC support) is the platform prerequisite; #19460 (bitcoin-wallet -ipcconnect) is downstream glue depending on #10102/#29409 and belongs after it.
#36796 is substantively a wallet-security change; only the SQLite depends recipe flag falls in this category, so its P4 here does not reflect its importance in wallet.
#36593 depends on #36592, which is not present in this category list; the dependency should be confirmed before review.
result.notes: The list is dominated by CI-coverage additions and compiler-warning enablement; the separating criterion applied was the category's own order of precedence (release/binary integrity, then supported-platform breakage, then CI reliability, then dependency transitions, then friction). Only two PRs address something that would ship a wrong or weakened binary (#35765, #36534); they are the clear P1s. Warning-flag and IWYU PRs were kept at P3 when they catch real defects and P4 when purely cosmetic.
